results.title: Measuring Systemic Banking Resilience: A Simple Reverse Stress Testing Approach
results.journal_or_venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper (Policy Research Working Paper 9864)
results.abstract_summary: The paper develops a simple, transparent country-level banking resilience metric called the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP), derived from bank-level reverse stress tests that estimate the rise in non-performing loans required to deplete capital buffers for the most fragile banks representing at least 20% of system assets. Applied to over 1,500 banks in 59 emerging and developing economies during the COVID-19 pandemic, the CDBP captures tail risks and appears to provide complementary information to standard macro-financial and financial soundness indicators, though it is limited in scope and should be complemented with additional supervisory data and stress tests.
results.methodology_description: The paper develops a simple, transparent reverse stress testing framework applied to bank-level accounting data to construct a country-level banking sector resilience metric called the Consolidated Distance to Break Point (CDBP). For each bank the authors compute a Break Point (BP) defined as the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio that would deplete the bank's regulatory capital down to the country minimum capital requirement (MCR), accounting for additional provisioning and the RWA impact of the non-provisioned portion of new NPLs. A constant provisioning rate for new NPLs (55%) is assumed (derived from an equal split among substandard, doubtful and loss categories with provisioning rates 20/50/100%), and provisions are assumed to be fully absorbed by capital (no profits used unless in a robustness variant). Bank-level Distance from Break Point (DBP) is BP minus current NPL (floored at zero). Banks are sorted by DBP and the subset of most fragile banks whose combined assets reach at least 20% of total banking system assets (the “Banks at Risk”) is selected. For that subset the authors compute consolidated BP (CBP) and the CDBP as gross-loan-weighted aggregates. The empirical application uses bank-level balance sheet data (primarily Fitch) for Q3 2020 (or the latest available not older than 2019) for about 1,500 commercial banks across 59 emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). The authors then analyze the cross-country distribution of CDBP, compare it to other indicators (EIU banking risk index, GDP growth, government debt) and run cross-sectional regressions of CDBP on IMF Financial Soundness Indicators (FSIs) and report robustness checks (including allowing minimal profits as an absorbing buffer). Key assumptions and limitations are stated (no collateral, no interbank contagion, focus on credit risk only, MCR from World Bank BRSS 2016, provisioning composition assumptions, etc.).
results.dataset_used: Bank-level balance sheet data from Fitch (Q3 2020 or latest ≤2019) for ~1,500 commercial banks in 59 EMDEs. Key variables: NPL ratio (% of gross loans), Total Regulatory Capital (USD), Risk-Weighted Assets (USD), Gross Loans (USD), Total Assets (USD). Country minimum capital requirements from World Bank Bank Regulation and Supervision Survey (year-end 2016). Supplementary country-level indicators: IMF Financial Soundness Indicators, EIU banking risk index, World Bank Global Economic Prospects and Macro-Fiscal Model DB.
results.experiment_input: Primary source: Fitch bank-level data for Q3 2020 (fallback to latest ≤2019) covering ~1,500 banks headquartered in 59 EMDEs. Supplementary sources: World Bank BRSS (MCR 2016), IMF FSIs, EIU banking risk, World Bank GDP and fiscal forecasts. Preprocessing steps: compute or extract NPL ratio, TRC, RWA, gross loans, total assets; compute aggregate risk-weight density as RWA/TotalAssets; enforce data freshness filter (no data older than 2019); drop or floor negative/invalid values as needed (not detailed); construct country banking system totals for asset-weighting.
results.experiment_process: 1) For each bank compute BP using the algebraic formula in the paper which equates TRC minus additional provisioning-induced capital reduction to MCR×RWA, while accounting for the change in RWA from the non-provisioned portion of new NPLs (using risk-weight density). 2) Assume provisioning rate for new NPLs = 55% (average of 20/50/100% across substandard/doubtful/loss). 3) Compute DBP = max(BP − current NPL, 0); set DBP=0 if bank already undercapitalized. 4) Sort banks by DBP (ascending), breaking ties by larger total assets first. 5) Select the subset of banks (Banks at Risk) whose cumulative assets reach at least 20% of the country’s banking system assets. 6) For Banks at Risk compute consolidated BP (CBP) and CDBP as gross-loan-weighted averages of bank-level BP and DBP respectively. 7) Produce cross-country distributions and regional summaries of CDBP. 8) Run cross-sectional OLS regressions of CDBP on selected FSIs and other macro variables to assess correlations and explanatory power; report coefficients, standard errors and R-squared. 9) Conduct robustness checks, notably including bank profits as a first absorbing buffer (using the minimum bank profit over a 10-year window in an alternative BP formula) and report pairwise correlations.
results.experiment_output: Primary outputs: bank-level BP and DBP; country-level CBP and CDBP (percentage-point increase in NPLs that would deplete capital for Banks at Risk). Descriptive outputs: distributions by World Bank region, medians, interquartile ranges, identification of countries where small NPL increases (e.g., 5 pp) would deplete capital. Comparative outputs: scatter plots of CDBP vs EIU banking risk index, GDP growth forecasts, and government debt. Inferential outputs: cross-sectional regression tables of CDBP on FSIs (coefficients, robust standard errors, R-squared), and robustness statistics including pairwise correlation (e.g., 0.953 between main CDBP and profit-included variant). No probabilistic likelihoods or time-to-failure horizons are produced; outputs are deterministic scenario thresholds.

experiment_parameters.profit_inclusion_robustness: minimum bank profit over 10-year period if used

results.reproducibility_notes: The methodology and formulas are fully described, enabling replication in principle. Major data inputs include proprietary Fitch bank-level data (coverage ~1,500 banks across 59 EMDEs), which may limit reproducibility for researchers without access to Fitch. Other input data (World Bank BRSS for MCRs, IMF FSIs, World Bank GDP/fiscal forecasts) are publicly available. No code repository or scripts are referenced in the paper. Reproducibility therefore requires access to the same commercial dataset and reimplementation of the algebraic calculations and aggregation steps; sensitivity to key assumptions (provisioning rate, profit inclusion, MCR treatment) is documented and can be varied by replicators.
key_findings: [supported] Introduces the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP), a simple country-level metric derived from bank-level reverse stress tests that measures the percentage-point increase in non-performing loans (NPLs) required to deplete capital buffers of the subset of most fragile banks representing at least 20% of total banking system assets.

[supported] Applies the CDBP methodology to an empirical sample of approximately 1,500 commercial banks across 59 emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) using Q3 2020 (or latest ≤2019) balance-sheet data.
[supported] Finds a median country CDBP of 9.8 percentage points (i.e., median consolidated NPL increase needed to deplete capital buffers for Banks at Risk).

[supported] Reports that in 10 countries a 5 percentage-point increase in NPLs would be sufficient to deplete capital buffers of Banks at Risk, and that two countries in the sample already had Banks at Risk that were undercapitalized.

[supported] Documents regional variation in CDBP: South Asia (SAR) shows the lowest median CDBP (~3.8 pp), Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) shows one of the highest median CDBPs (~14.0 pp), and East Asia & Pacific (EAP) shows a tighter distribution.

[supported] Cross-sectional regressions indicate a limited association between CDBP and commonly used Financial Soundness Indicators (FSIs): modest statistical relationships, low explanatory power (R-squared values generally low), a positive association with liquidity (liquid assets to short-term liabilities) and a negative association with interest margin to gross income.
[supported] Sensitivity test incorporating bank profits as an initial buffer produces very similar CDBP values (pairwise correlation between original and profits-included CDBP = 0.953).

[supported] Method relies on explicit, reportable assumptions (e.g., uniform provisioning rate of 55% for new NPLs, no collateral assumed, no profits unless explicitly added, use of country minimum capital requirement from BRSS 2016).

[supported] The authors acknowledge multiple limitations of the CDBP: it focuses solely on credit risk, does not capture interbank contagion or non-linear dependencies, omits FX/liquidity/sovereign-bank nexus risks, says little about likelihood or timing of NPL increases, and depends on potentially lagged or underreported NPL data and incomplete bank coverage.

[speculative] The authors claim the CDBP encapsulates complementary information to traditional macro-financial and soundness indicators and could therefore be a useful input for basic monitoring in data-limited environments.
[speculative] The CDBP could be used as an off-site screening tool to flag banking sectors that warrant more in-depth supervisory risk reviews (asset quality reviews, on-site inspections).

[speculative] Reverse stress testing that maps increases in NPLs into provisioning needs and capital depletion is particularly useful during crises (e.g., COVID-19) when balance-sheet transparency is reduced due to forbearance and policy measures.
results.results_summary: The paper develops the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP), a transparent reverse-stress-testing based metric that quantifies the percentage-point rise in non-performing loans that would deplete capital buffers for the group of most vulnerable banks that together represent at least 20% of system assets. Applied to ~1,500 banks in 59 EMDEs (Q3 2020 / latest ≤2019), the median country CDBP is 9.8 percentage points, with substantial cross-country and regional heterogeneity (e.g., SAR lower, SSA higher). Cross-sectional analysis shows only modest correlations between CDBP and standard financial soundness indicators, suggesting complementary information content. Sensitivity tests (including profits) yield highly correlated results. The authors emphasize the metric's simplicity and potential usefulness for preliminary surveillance in data-constrained settings, while also clearly listing important limitations (no contagion channels, single-risk focus, data quality and coverage concerns).
performance_claims: Sample: ~1,500 commercial banks across 59 EMDEs (data Q3 2020 or latest ≤2019).
In 10 countries, a 5 percentage-point increase in NPLs would deplete capital buffers of Banks at Risk.
Two countries in the sample had Banks at Risk already undercapitalized at the time of measurement.
Regional medians: SAR ~3.8 pp (lowest), SSA ~14.0 pp (one of the highest), (EAP median CDBP ~13.6 pp reported as region example).

Assumed provisioning rate for new NPLs = 55% (average based on 20%/50%/100% for substandard/doubtful/loss categories).
Banks at Risk defined as the most fragile banks that collectively represent at least 20% of banking system assets.
results.quantum_advantage_detail: The paper is focused on bank-sector reverse stress testing and the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint metric for assessing banking resilience. It makes no claims about quantum computing or any quantum advantage; therefore quantum-related classification is not applicable.
limitations: Focuses only on credit risk and does not account for other important risk types (liquidity, foreign exchange, market risk, sovereign-bank nexus, sudden stops, commodity price volatility).
Does not capture interbank linkages, non-linear distress dependencies, contagion, or knock-on/balance-sheet feedback effects.
Does not attach any likelihood or probability to the computed increase in NPLs nor specify a time horizon over which the shock materializes.
Assumes increases in provisioning are fully absorbed by regulatory capital (initially assumes no profits to cover provisions).
Does not consider tax implications (e.g., tax credits) that could mitigate capital impacts.

Assumes a fixed NPL provisioning rate (55%) derived from an equal split across substandard, doubtful, and loss categories and fixed provisioning rates; ignores country- or bank-specific provisioning regimes.
Ignores collateral: provisioning is applied to the entire NPL exposure without accounting for the value of collateral or supervisory haircuts.
Assumes the same (aggregate) risk-weight density for original loans and uses a simplified mapping to RWA impacts.

Minimum capital requirement data are taken from 2016 and are applied equally to all banks; the approach does not incorporate bank-specific or time-varying additional capital buffers (e.g., capital conservation buffer, systemic buffers) or other constraints such as leverage ratio requirements.
NPL data are backward-looking, subject to reporting lags, and may be underreported or distorted (especially under regulatory forbearance), reducing reliability of results.
Sample coverage may be incomplete or biased: unlisted banks (mutual or state-owned), smaller banks, rural credit institutions, and other credit institutions may be missing or undercovered.
The 20% banking-assets threshold to define 'Banks at Risk' is a choice that may not be appropriate for all jurisdictions and may need adjustment based on banking-sector granularity.
Aggregate consolidation over 'Banks at Risk' may obscure heterogeneity across banks and other bank-level vulnerabilities not captured by the metric.
[inferred] Static, single-period snapshot: metric does not model dynamics or the evolution of vulnerabilities over time.
[inferred] Sensitive to data vintage and source (use of Fitch and mixing 2019 and 2020 data could introduce inconsistencies).
[inferred] The metric does not integrate market-based indicators or forward-looking signals, which may limit early-warning capabilities.
[inferred] Simplifying modeling choices (e.g., how RWA responds to newly non-performing exposures) may misstate capital impacts in jurisdictions with different regulatory treatments.
open_questions: How should the provisioning rate and NPL composition be calibrated to reflect country- and bank-specific accounting and supervisory regimes?
How would the CDBP change if collateral values and supervisory haircuts were incorporated (i.e., not assuming zero collateral)?
How sensitive is the CDBP to the choice of the 'Banks at Risk' threshold (20% of assets), and how should that threshold be chosen for different banking-system structures?
How can interbank linkages, contagion channels, and second-round effects be incorporated into a similar (data-light) reverse stress testing framework?
What is the likelihood (probability) of the NPL increases implied by the CDBP in different macroeconomic scenarios, and over what time horizon would such increases materialize?
How should bank profits and tax credits be best incorporated into the absorbing-buffer assumption across countries and through crisis cycles?
How robust is the CDBP to data quality issues and reporting lags, particularly under episodes of regulatory forbearance?
Can the CDBP be combined with market-based or macro-financial indicators to improve predictive power or early-warning capacity?
How should bank-specific capital buffers (e.g., systemic risk buffers, CCyB) and leverage constraints be reflected in the minimum capital benchmark used?
How can the approach be adapted to capture other relevant shocks for EMDEs (sovereign distress, FX depreciation, capital flow reversals, commodity price shocks)?
What supervisory actions or policy responses are implied when a country shows a low/high CDBP, and how should authorities prioritize follow-up (e.g., on-site inspections, asset quality reviews)?
future_work: Relax key assumptions: incorporate bank profits (and scenarios for profitability), tax effects, and country- or bank-specific provisioning practices when data permit.
Adapt the provisioning and RWA-impact calculations to account for collateral, supervisory haircuts, and jurisdictional accounting rules.
Allow the minimum capital requirement to vary by bank and over time to reflect additional capital buffers (capital conservation buffer, systemic buffers, leverage ratio requirements).
Explore alternative thresholds for defining 'Banks at Risk' and tailor the threshold to country banking-sector granularity.
Integrate the CDBP with other stress testing tools and supervisory information (on-site inspections, asset quality reviews) to create a multi-layered assessment suitable for low-data environments.
Extend the framework to incorporate other shock types (sovereign-bank nexus, FX risk, liquidity shocks, commodity price shocks) and multi-risk scenarios.
Develop approaches to capture interbank exposures, contagion, and non-linear dependencies in a data-constrained setting.
Attach probabilities or scenario-based likelihoods and explicit time horizons to the NPL increases implied by the reverse stress test.
Assess robustness of the metric across data vintages and sources, and improve coverage of unlisted/smaller banks and non-bank financial institutions.
Combine the CDBP with market-based indicators and macro-financial variables to evaluate its incremental predictive power for banking distress.
key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Proposes the Consolidated Distance to Break Point (CDBP), a simple, transparent country-level banking resilience metric built from bank-level reverse stress tests and applied to ~1,500 banks in 59 EMDEs using Fitch balance-sheet data.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Combines bank-level algebraic reverse-stress calculations (Break Point, DBP) with asset-weighted aggregation to identify a subset of 'Banks at Risk' (those whose combined assets reach 20% of the system) and compute consolidated indicators (CBP, CDBP), plus robustness variants (e.g., include profit buffers).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Generates deterministic threshold outputs and cross-sectional regression evidence linking CDBP to existing financial soundness indicators; methodology is implementable with access to commercial bank-level data but subject to strong simplifying assumptions (no collateral, no interbank contagion, fixed provisioning rules).
